organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Took over Afghanistan in Aug 2021. It is not monolithic; it has pragmatist and hardliner factions. It denies a foreign fighter presence but has been trying to register foreign fighters.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Deliberately took control of many portfolios in the de facto authority; controls the Interior Ministry.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Lacks developed external operations capability. Likely to gain freedom of movement and safe haven under the Taliban.

organizations.name: AQIS
organizations.notes: Fought alongside the Taliban in the 2021 takeover.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: Lost its emir in Feb 2022 and its deputy and finance chief in 2021; faces a succession and announcement dilemma. Maintains core functions (military, security, finance, ideology, propaganda).

organizations.name: ISIS Khorasan Province
organizations.notes: Possible destination for disaffected Taliban members.

organizations.name: ISIS West Africa Province
organizations.notes: Largest ISIS affiliate outside Iraq and Syria by fighter numbers; split from Boko Haram. Hub for ISGS.

organizations.name: Boko Haram
organizations.notes: Led by Shekau until his death; remnants are being only partially absorbed by ISWAP.

organizations.name: ISIS Greater Sahara
organizations.notes: Based in the Mali–Niger–Burkina Faso tri-border area; assessed as a spoke dependent on the ISWAP hub.

organizations.name: Ansar Bayt al-Maqdis
organizations.notes: ISIS-affiliated group in Sinai; has had little recent success because of effective counter-terrorism.

organizations.name: UN 1267 Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: Edmund Fitton-Brown is its coordinator. The 29th report covers June–December 2021.

organizations.name: Iraqi security forces
organizations.notes: Captured Samuel al-Jaburi.

organizations.name: Eastern Turkistan Islamic Party
organizations.notes: A foreign jihadist group in Afghanistan; the Taliban looks to integrate some such groups.

organizations.name: Islamic Jihad Union
organizations.notes: A Central Asian foreign jihadist group in Afghanistan.

organizations.name: Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan
organizations.notes: Described as 'back' in the UN report.

organizations.name: Ansar al-Sunna wa Jama'a
organizations.notes: ISIS-pledged group in northern Mozambique; the transcript cuts off while describing March 2021 events.

organizations.name: Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan
organizations.notes: Roggio refers only obliquely to 'movement of Taliban in Pakistan'.

organizations.name: ISWAP (Islamic State West Africa Province)
organizations.notes: Based in the Lake Chad Basin; hub for the ISGS 'spoke'. Attacks in Cameroon, Niger and Chad. UN is concerned about its growth.

organizations.name: ISGS (Islamic State Greater Sahara)
organizations.notes: Further west; effectively a spoke that reports to or depends on ISWAP.

organizations.name: ISIL core
organizations.notes: Has a Directorate of Provinces. A regional leader may have returned to the role of regional representative of ISIL core.

organizations.name: ISIL Somalia / Puntland hub
organizations.notes: Hub of an ISIL structure linking Somalia, northern Mozambique and eastern DRC. Funding and support flow from Somalia to Mozambique and the DRC.

organizations.name: Ansar al-Sunna wa Jama'a (ASWJ)
organizations.notes: Pledged allegiance to ISIL. Not directly related to Somalia's al-Shabaab. Expanded in northern Mozambique in 2021, with some counter-terrorist pushback.

organizations.name: Allied Democratic Forces (ADF)
organizations.notes: Active in DRC, Uganda and Rwanda. Leadership pledged to ISIL; one faction rejects this.

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
organizations.notes: Described as possibly al-Qaeda's strongest franchise worldwide. Strong revenue raising through extortion. Regular attacks in Kenya. Controlled most of southern and central Somalia 2007-2011. Praised the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan.

organizations.name: Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM)
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda-aligned coalition. Strong in Mali and Burkina Faso, spilling into Niger and the Mali/Senegal/Côte d'Ivoire border areas. Pursues a long-term radicalization strategy. Its predecessor controlled central Mali 2011-2012.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM)
organizations.notes: North African franchise, tends to be Algerian. Overlord of JNIM and connection point to al-Qaeda leadership.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP)
organizations.notes: Tried to hold territory in Yemen but never succeeded; much weaker than al-Shabaab.

organizations.name: UN Monitoring Team
aliases: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: Coordinated by Edmund Fitton-Brown. Latest report discussed.

organizations.name: African Union troops in Somalia
organizations.notes: About 22,000 troops; Roggio says they are the main factor holding al-Shabaab back.

organizations.name: ISIL Philippines
organizations.notes: Damaged by its defeat at Marawi.

events.description: Amin al-Haq returned to Afghanistan and his home in Nangarhar to a Taliban-escorted parade; also seen in Kabul.
The Taliban took over Afghanistan with AQIS fighting alongside them.
Last proof-of-life video of Ayman al-Zawahiri.
Abu Muhammad al-Masri assassinated in Tehran with his daughter (previously reported).
Iraqi forces captured ISIS finance chief and deputy Samuel al-Jaburi (announced Oct/Nov 2021).
Hasakah prison break by ISIS in northeastern Syria shortly before Abu Ibrahim was killed.
ISIS emir Abu Ibrahim al-Hashimi al-Qurashi killed ('we just had the death of the Islamic State's emir', episode published 15 Feb 2022).
Fall of the last ISIS territory at Baghouz; detainees and families moved to camps.
Shekau killed himself in Sambisa Forest when tracked down by ISWAP.
Unconfirmed reports that Barnawi was killed.
ASWJ/ISIS-linked events in northern Mozambique; the transcript cuts off before detail.
The UN Monitoring Team's 29th (1267) report was released, covering June–December 2021.

key_claims: The Taliban takeover has made Afghanistan more of a safe haven for al-Qaeda and foreign fighters; the UN report says terrorist groups enjoy greater freedom there than at any time in recent history.
Amin al-Haq's escorted parade in Nangarhar shows Taliban comfort with al-Qaeda figures, making a return by Saif al-Adel or Zawahiri less problematic for the Taliban.
Sirajuddin Haqqani and his family control the Interior Ministry and special units, so the odds of the Taliban suppressing al-Qaeda are very low.
The Taliban are better described as pragmatist versus hardline than moderate; the Haqqanis are pragmatists with an al-Qaeda relationship.
Zawahiri is in poor health, and a succession to Saif al-Adel is a live question. His death might go unacknowledged to avoid a coronation problem.
The capture of ISIS deputy and finance chief Samuel al-Jaburi followed by the killing of Abu Ibrahim was a one-two leadership blow; the Hasakah jailbreak and a courier may have been factors.
ISIS must announce a new emir and secure pledges from provinces, but its past policy of hiding Abu Ibrahim failed to keep him safe.
A camp in northeastern Syria is treated by ISIS as an administrative unit, processing remittances for people in Syria and Iraq.
ISWAP is the largest ISIS affiliate outside Iraq and Syria, and ISGS appears dependent on it.
The UN assesses that ISGS is a spoke dependent on the ISWAP hub in the Lake Chad Basin, and that ISWAP is growing stronger and could become more ambitious.
ISIL has a Somalia/Puntland hub that links its presence in northern Mozambique and eastern DRC through support and finance.
Al-Shabaab may be al-Qaeda's strongest franchise worldwide, with strong revenue raising and an international terrorist aspiration.
JNIM, an al-Qaeda-aligned coalition overseen by AQIM, is spreading from Mali into Burkina Faso and the littoral states through a long-term radicalization strategy.
AQIM's Droukdel was killed in 2020, and his successor is believed to be in North Africa rather than the Sahel.
Roggio says the AU troops in Somalia are the main factor holding al-Shabaab back from retaking territory.
Southeast Asia is a bright spot: arrests, the killing of ISIL's reported regional leader, and COVID constraints have set the groups back.
Threat levels in non-conflict zones are relatively low, since ISIL and al-Qaeda lack external operations capability.
